claims.text: Nanoscale multilayer interfaces and sluggish diffusion act synergistically to impede dislocation motion in high-entropy-alloy coatings.
Impeded dislocation motion delays creep nucleation and propagation.
Delayed creep nucleation and propagation confer resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation.
Nanoscale interfaces generate misfit stresses and lattice distortions.
Interface-generated misfit stresses and lattice distortions disrupt dislocation glide.
Slow atomic diffusion is intrinsic to high-entropy alloys.
Multilayer interfaces block or increase the complexity of dislocation pathways.
Localized interface stress fields combined with sluggish diffusion delay dislocation accumulation.
Localized interface stress fields combined with sluggish diffusion delay creep-strain development relative to a homogeneous alloy.
Under identical creep-test temperature and load, multilayer high-entropy-alloy coatings will accumulate plastic strain at a significantly lower rate than homogeneous coatings of the same composition.
Homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coatings are expected to exhibit a higher rate of time-dependent plastic deformation than multilayer coatings under identical temperature and load.
The proposed mechanism applies at moderate-to-high temperatures below melting where diffusion and dislocation motion are active.
The proposed mechanism may cease to govern at extreme strain rates or temperatures where alternative deformation mechanisms dominate.
A controlled comparison should use multilayer and homogeneous coatings with identical alloy compositions under the same constant-load creep conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if multilayer coatings show no statistically significant reduction in creep strain relative to homogeneous coatings.
The hypothesis is also falsified if microstructural analysis reveals no interface-mediated dislocation hindrance relative to homogeneous samples.
